newsitem.title: BELGIUM: TV sport for all is EU's aim.
newsitem.headline: TV sport for all is EU's aim.

text.p: The European Commission will propose next week changing EU law make sure everyone can see live television coverage of major sporting events like the soccer World Cup and the Olympic Games.
Under a proposed amendment to the EU's television without frontiers law, pay television channels like BSKYB and Canal Plus would still be able to buy exclusive rights to sports events.
But they would have to respect laws laid down in individual European Union countries saying specified events must be broadcast free either uncoded or on a non-pay channel.
"The rules concern not the acquisition, but the use of the rights," said one EU official.
"The main objective is to ensure that events of major importance for society are on the clear (non-encrypted) television and not pay television."
Last July, for example, Germany's Kirch group won a bidding battle for television rights to the 2002 and 2006 World Cup Soccer Finals.

The move by the EU executive, which EU officials say is backed by most member states, responds to European Parliament demands that the right of rich and poor alike to watch big sports events should be protected.
Under the proposal broadcasters would have to respect national lists of important sporting events and show them uncoded.
At present only three EU member countries -- Britain. France and Belgium -- have such lists, but as a result of the EU move other countries could draw them up, EU officials said.

In Britain soccer events like the FA Cup Final, the Scottish FA Cup Final and the FIFA World Cup Final are on the list along with the racing events the Derby and Grand National, the Olympic Games, the Wimbledon Tennis Championships and Cricket Test Matches involving England.

On France's list are the Summer and Winter Olympics, the Tour de France cycle race, European Cup football matches, Five Nations rugby union matches in which the French national team takes part, and the French football cup final.
In Belgium's Flemish region a new list is drawn up every year.
EU officials said that even in cases where national law obliged the pay television stations to show the events free, they would still get the benefit from advertising and sponsorship.
They could also sell the events to other television channels in the country concerned, they said.
A Commission document made available to Reuters stresses that the new proposal, which is on the Commission agenda for next Wednesday, would only apply to a small proportion of sports events.

"It should be pointed out that national measures often concern only major events, the number of which is by definition limited and not the whole field of sports or other programme rights," the paper said.
It said that in Britain the listed events represent less than one percent of all televised sport.
To take effect, the proposal would have to be formally agreed by EU culture ministers.
